title: The AI That Keeps Working After You Close the App: Always-On Agents, Explained
summary: A new generation of AI agents keeps working while you sleep. Before you hand one your inbox, know what it can do unsupervised, what it remembers, and which permissions stick.
before: You ask a question, you get an answer. Close the app and nothing happens until you come back.
after: The AI keeps researching, scheduling, and drafting in the background - then pings you when it needs approval.
body:
For fifteen years, talking to AI meant waiting for a reply. You asked, it answered, you closed the tab. That model is ending. A new wave of products - OpenAI's dots, Meta's Muse, Apple's upgraded Siri, and startups like Instinct - keeps working after you walk away. They run on their own cloud computers, monitor your connected apps, and bring back results for approval. It is a genuine shift in what consumer AI can do. It is also a shift in what you are trusting it with.

## What Changed: From Chatbot to Persistent Agent

A chatbot waits for your next prompt. An always-on agent does not. It has ongoing responsibilities - scanning your inbox for unbilled invoices, watching for flight delays, preparing a morning calendar summary - and it handles them whether you are at your desk or asleep.

OpenAI calls its version **dots**. Announced at DevDay on September 29, 2026, a dot runs on GPT-6 Astra with its own cloud computer and browser. It can connect to more than 4,000 apps and keeps working between conversations. Meta's **Muse**, which launched three weeks earlier, does the same through WhatsApp and a dedicated app: it books travel, sends emails, and makes purchases using Stripe Link. Apple's Siri upgrade, shown at WWDC 2026, promises multi-step tasks with on-screen awareness. The startup **Instinct**, valued at $10 billion as of late September, lets you text or call an agent that then operates a computer on your behalf.

These are not the same product, but they share an architecture: a persistent agent with memory, app access, and the ability to act without a live prompt. If you want to understand where consumer AI is heading, this is it.

## How They Keep You in the Loop (Mostly)

The companies building these agents know the obvious worry: what happens when software with access to your email and calendar does something you did not intend?

OpenAI's answer involves a distinction between **reading** and **acting**. When a dot is scanning your apps in the background - what OpenAI calls proactive research - its tools are restricted to read-only access. It cannot send messages, change app content, or control a browser without your involvement. User-directed tasks and scheduled jobs can act, but under separate rules and approval gates you configure.

Meta's Muse asks for approval before sending emails or making purchases. Instinct revised its terms after early testers flagged issues, including an email that went out without confirmation. The pattern across all of them is the same: background work is constrained, consequential actions require a check-in.

These are guardrails, not guarantees. OpenAI's own safety documentation notes that dots "can still make mistakes, including when following your rules." But the architecture is designed so that the agent cannot, for example, empty your bank account while you are not looking.

## Three Things to Check Before You Use One

If you are considering handing an agent your inbox, calendar, or credit card, here are the questions worth asking first.

**1. What can it do unattended?**

Know the difference between read-only background research and authorized actions. For dots, proactive research cannot send messages or modify content. Purchases, permanent deletions, and password changes always require your approval. Check the equivalent rules for any agent you connect.

**2. What does it remember - and how do you delete it?**

A dot builds its own memory from your conversations and connected apps. Here is the sharp edge: disconnecting an app stops new access, but it does not erase what the dot already learned. The only way to clear a dot's memory is to delete the dot entirely, which also deletes its conversations and scheduled tasks. OpenAI's help center is direct: "You currently cannot view, delete or directly modify individual dot memories."

Meta says Muse users can ask it to forget specific things, though Meta describes that as "best-effort" - it may still remember information it learned from what you deleted. Before you connect anything sensitive, understand the deletion policy.

**3. What permissions cannot be turned off?**

Every agent has a floor of access that comes with using it. For dots, work started in Codex or ChatGPT Work counts against your plan's usage limits. For Muse, Meta uses queries for model training by default, though users can opt out. Read the terms - not just the marketing - to know what you are agreeing to.

## The Price of Entry

These agents are not free. OpenAI's dots require at least a ChatGPT Pro subscription at $100 a month; Pro users in the EU, UK, and Switzerland do not get access at launch. Meta's Muse has a free tier with limited tokens, plus paid plans at $20 and $100 a month. Instinct is invite-only and has not published pricing. Apple's Siri upgrade will ship with iOS 27 this fall, included in the devices people already own.

For more context on the business models behind these products, see our article on agentic-ai-explained.

## The Bottom Line

Always-on agents represent a real capability jump - not hype, not science fiction, but software that can handle ongoing work while you do something else. They are also a new category of trust. The question is not whether these tools are useful. It is whether you understand what you are handing them before you click connect.
